title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect the pipe's process function to its structural load-transfer role.
student: What are the primary process and structural functions of the pipe-turbine assembly?
instructor: The pipe transfers steam between turbine housings while maintaining a sealed connection. Structurally, it transfers thermally induced axial loads into the turbine attachments when free thermal deformation is restrained.
gradingNotes: Good answers should mention both fluid transport and mechanical load transfer.

title: Source of Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Distinguish thermal loading from a directly applied force.
student: What creates the mechanical loading in this problem? Is an independent external axial force applied to the pipe?
instructor: The temperature change causes the pipe to seek a free length change αLΔT. Finite restraint at the turbine attachments opposes that change and creates axial force. No independent external axial load is applied in the base model.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Interpret finite attachment stiffness as partial axial restraint.
student: Identify the support idealization used for turbine attachments A and B.
instructor: Each turbine attachment is modeled as an axial linear spring of stiffness k. The pipe ends are therefore partially restrained and can move as the attachments deform under the thermally induced force.
commonMistakes: The attachment points are not perfectly fixed in this model.

title: Thermal Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace thermally induced force from the pipe into the foundation.
student: Trace the load path created when thermal deformation of the pipe is restrained.
instructor: The pipe attempts to change length; the turbine attachments resist that motion; axial force develops in the pipe; equal and opposite forces pass through the flanged connections into the turbine housings, machine supports, and foundation.

title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Identify components controlling the one-dimensional response.
student: Which components are most important for this simplified Mechanics of Materials analysis?
instructor: The hollow steel pipe is critical because it develops axial stress, and the two turbine attachments are critical because their stiffness controls the degree of restraint. Detailed flange, bolt, gasket, casing, and foundation stresses are not evaluated.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Select force and stress responses supported by the provided data.
student: What mechanical responses should be evaluated in the base problem?
instructor: Evaluate thermally induced axial force and average axial pipe stress. Comparing stress with yield provides a limited strength interpretation. Pressure stress, creep, fatigue, local flange response, bending, and stability require additional models and data.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect each input to thermal deformation, axial compliance, or strength.
student: Identify the geometric, thermal, material, and support parameters that control the pipe force and stress.
instructor: The required inputs are pipe length L, outer diameter Do, wall thickness t, temperatures T1 and T2, attachment stiffness k, elastic modulus E, thermal-expansion coefficient α, and yield stress σy. Inner diameter and area follow from the pipe geometry.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the plant assembly into a one-dimensional thermal compatibility model.
student: Before using the reference figure, develop a simplified mechanics model showing the hollow pipe, turbine attachment points, axial support stiffness, pipe length, temperature change, and unknown thermally induced axial force.
instructor: A correct idealization shows a uniform hollow pipe of length L connected between two axial springs, each of stiffness k. The pipe has free thermal deformation αLΔT, but attachment restraint creates axial force.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before the instructor reference idealization is revealed.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the thermal compatibility solution.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real pipe-turbine assembly into the simplified model.
instructor: Typical assumptions are uniform pipe temperature; a uniform hollow cross section; one-dimensional axial behavior; linear-elastic pipe material and supports; identical attachment stiffness at A and B; small deformation; rigid flange load transfer; and neglected pressure, bending, thermal gradients, creep, fatigue, routing flexibility, and local connection effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the calculation from geometry through engineering interpretation.
student: Before calculating, describe the sequence needed to determine the force exerted on the turbine housings.
instructor: Compute inner diameter and pipe area; determine ΔT and free thermal deformation; write compatibility among free deformation, pipe elastic deformation, and both support displacements; solve for axial force; compute average pipe stress; compare with yield; then state a limited recommendation.

title: Boundary Conditions from the Reference Diagram
student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the pipe boundary conditions and support idealizations.
instructor: Pipe AB is connected at each end to a turbine attachment modeled as an axial spring of stiffness k. Both attachment points can move under force, so the pipe is partially rather than fully restrained.

title: Unknown Thermally Induced Force
learningObjectives: Define the unknown interaction force and its action on each component.
student: Identify the unknown axial force produced by restrained thermal deformation and describe its action on the pipe and turbine housings.
instructor: The unknown is the thermally induced axial pipe force. For the assigned temperatures, the pipe is in {{thermal_force_state}} and exerts equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces on the two turbine attachments.

title: Hollow-Pipe Cross-Sectional Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the material area of a hollow circular section.
student: For Do = {{D_o}} {{D_o_unit}} and t = {{t}} {{t_unit}}, determine the inner diameter and cross-sectional area of the steel pipe.
commonMistakes: Use the annular material area, not the area of a solid bar with diameter Do.

title: Free Thermal Deformation
student: Calculate the temperature change and the pipe deformation that would occur if the pipe were unrestrained.
instructor:
ΔT = T2 - T1 = {{T_2}} - {{T_1}} = {{thermal_delta_T_F}}°F. The pipe experiences {{thermal_action}}.

δT = αLΔT = {{thermal_free_expansion_in}} in, with magnitude {{thermal_free_expansion_magnitude_in}} in.
gradingNotes: A positive value denotes free expansion; a negative value denotes free contraction.

title: Compatibility Equation
learningObjectives: Formulate compatibility for a member between two flexible supports.
student: Write the signed compatibility equation relating free thermal deformation, elastic deformation of the pipe, and movement of both turbine attachments.
instructor:
Using a compression-positive sign convention for F,

αLΔT = FL/(AE) + 2F/k.

The pipe compliance is {{thermal_pipe_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip, the combined support compliance is {{thermal_support_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip, and total compliance is {{thermal_total_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip. The factor 2 accounts for movement at both turbine attachments.
commonMistakes: Do not omit one attachment displacement or treat the two end springs as a single spring of stiffness k.

title: Thermally Induced Pipe Force
learningObjectives: Solve compatibility for the pipe-support interaction force.
student: Solve for the thermally induced axial force in the pipe and the force magnitude exerted on each turbine housing.
instructor:
F = δT/[L/(AE) + 2/k] = {{thermal_pipe_force_kip}} kip using compression-positive thermal-force convention. Thus the pipe carries {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip in {{thermal_force_state}} and exerts that force magnitude on each turbine attachment.

The pipe elastic contribution has magnitude {{thermal_pipe_elastic_deformation_in}} in. Each support moves {{thermal_support_displacement_each_in}} in, for a combined support movement of {{thermal_support_displacement_total_in}} in.

title: Pipe Stress and Yield Comparison
learningObjectives: Calculate average axial stress and make a limited yield comparison.
student: Determine the average axial stress in the pipe and compare its magnitude with σy = {{sigma_y}} {{sigma_y_unit}}.
instructor: σ = F/A = {{thermal_pipe_stress_ksi}} ksi; its magnitude is {{thermal_pipe_stress_magnitude_ksi}} ksi in {{thermal_stress_state}}. The yield-to-stress ratio is {{thermal_yield_ratio}}. {{thermal_yield_assessment}}
gradingNotes: This is an average axial-stress comparison, not a pressure-piping code assessment or a full factor of safety evaluation.

title: Stiffness Interpretation
learningObjectives: Predict how support stiffness changes thermal force.
student: Explain how attachment stiffness k affects the thermal force. Which compliance contribution dominates for the assigned values?
instructor: Larger k permits less attachment movement, restrains more thermal deformation, and increases pipe force toward the fully restrained limit. Smaller k reduces force by allowing more movement. For the assigned values, {{thermal_dominant_compliance}} is the larger compliance contribution.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a mechanics-based recommendation without overclaiming safety.
student: Use the force and stress results to make a limited engineering recommendation. Identify additional checks required before accepting the installation.
instructor: The pipe develops {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip in {{thermal_force_state}} and an average stress magnitude of {{thermal_pipe_stress_magnitude_ksi}} ksi. {{thermal_yield_assessment}} The turbine allowable nozzle loads should be compared with the computed attachment force. If more flexibility is needed, consider pipe-routing flexibility, engineered expansion provisions, or less rigid attachments. Final acceptance also requires pressure, flange, bolt, gasket, weld, creep, fatigue, thermal-gradient, stability, and code checks.
gradingNotes: The response should not claim full design safety from the average axial-stress calculation alone.
